ai-at-work.title: Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it’s not having one
ai-at-work.excerpt: With tech outages seemingly everywhere, Google took the unusual step of announcing that Gmail is working just fine, actually.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Google basically sent out a press release to tell everyone their email service wasn't broken, which is exactly as weird as it sounds. For digital workplace pros who've spent the last few years dealing with Teams crashes and Slack meltdowns, this announcement is oddly reassuring and deeply depressing at the same time. Only in 2024 do we celebrate major tech companies for the bare minimum of not falling apart, and honestly, Google probably got more PR value from this than they would have from an actual outage.

Here's the thing though: bankers have been saying they want automation for thirty years, but they also want to control every decimal point, so I'll believe this changes actual workflows when I see it.

After 30 years watching IT teams improvise solutions, I'll say this: watching infrastructure vendors finally admit that shell scripts and duct tape don't cut it at scale is oddly satisfying, even if it does mean your ops team needs retraining.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: CloudBackend just raised 6.6 million euros to help companies turn those AI-generated prototype apps into actual working business software that people can rely on. tools-tech.title: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026, plus more AI workplace updates
tools-tech.excerpt: The company also released new ROI tracking tools for companies monitoring their AI spend.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft rolled out Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026 and added fresh ROI tracking tools so companies can actually measure what they're spending on AI and whether it's worth the money. This matters because most organizations throwing cash at AI adoption have been flying blind on actual returns, and finance teams need real numbers to justify the spend to leadership. Here's the thing though: tracking ROI only helps if you're honest about the results, and I've seen plenty of companies massage the metrics to justify decisions they've already made.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?
tools-tech.excerpt: With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft could reshape enterprise spending, but there’s a critical difference between estimated value and money saved.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft is launching Agent 365 Business Analytics to quantify AI's financial impact on enterprise work, claiming it can show you exactly how much money your AI investments are saving you. This matters because digital workplace leaders are drowning in ROI questions from CFOs and executives who want hard numbers before they green light more AI spending. Here's the thing though: Microsoft showing you a dollar figure for AI productivity gains is like your car's fuel efficiency calculator telling you that you're actually getting 47 miles per gallon when you're really getting 28. The math will look good on the PowerPoint, but I'd want an independent audit before I start planning my next budget around it.

For digital workplace folks, this means your organization's AI tooling costs could drop dramatically, and the vendor lock-in dynamics that have felt pretty solid are suddenly very much in play. After 30 years watching Microsoft play this game, I'll believe it when I see enterprise customers actually running these models in production without the usual caveats and gotchas buried in the fine print.

digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece about people struggling to mentally disconnect from work stress, recommending wind-down routines as the antidote. This matters to digital workplace pros because we've built the always-on infrastructure that makes this problem worse, so understanding the human cost of our tools is literally our job. Here's the thing though: no amount of breathing exercises fixes a broken culture, and if your company expects you to "psychologically clock out" while Slack notifications ping all evening, you're treating the symptom, not the disease.

digital-culture.title: All these outages show how corporate America needs to modernize out-of-date tech
digital-culture.excerpt: Over the past five days, a string of high-profile tech outages has left Americans struggling to send emails, catch flights, and access their bank accounts. While the disruptions raised concerns about
digital-culture.dwp_take: Corporate America got hit with a cascade of major tech outages across banking, airlines, and email because their infrastructure is running on systems that should've been retired years ago. This matters to digital workplace pros because you're probably managing similar legacy tech debt in your own organizations, and these outages prove that neglecting modernization isn't just a "someday" problem anymore. The irony is priceless: everyone's worried about AI villains when the real enemy is the Windows server humming in the basement that nobody dares to touch.

digital-culture.title: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy feared being ‘a lousy dad’—so he did this
digital-culture.excerpt: When Amazon CEO Andy Jassy became a parent for the first time 26 years ago, he didn’t want to choose between being a good worker and being a good father. That left him with only one option. “I realize
digital-culture.dwp_take: Andy Jassy restructured his work approach after becoming a father 26 years ago to avoid being absent from his kids' lives. This matters because it's a rare admission from a Fortune 500 CEO that you can't actually do it all, and that intentional boundary setting requires real changes to how you work, not just saying you support work-life balance. The irony of course is that most of us don't get to reshape our jobs the way a CEO can, so this is heartwarming but also kind of proves the point that flexibility is still a privilege.
